utterances.speaker: WITNESS M [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure if that was the first time, but I know that I did mention it. MR. DI FAZIO: If Your Honours please, that last question, I wonder if Mr. Lazarevic is in possession of all of the material. I mean, this business of disclosure is important, of course, and I wonder if he's in possession of the notes from July of 1998. It may be of assistance to him in this line of cross-examination on the previous or the absence of these -- alleged absence of these matters in previous statements and utterances given to investigators. Indeed, it puts to the witness it wasn't until July 2001 that that was the first time the incident was mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, that was my question, but to be honest, I have never received any notes taken in 1998. I got two statements -- actually, this is one statement that was given in two days, on 14 and 17. Then after that I received, just before the trial started, the notes taken in July 2001. And these are -- and finally, I have received notes taken by my learned colleague just before this witness started his testifying, and these are in -- handwritten. Other notes, notes taken in 1998, I have never received. Of course, you caught me in this moment. I must confirm with other colleagues of mine, because I can just say in my name. But obviously, I mean all my colleagues said that they have never received any such notes. Of course, they would be very helpful, particularly in this course of cross-examination, but there is, I believe, another issue with regard to this. MR. DI FAZIO: They may well be. In fact, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Di Fazio. MR. DI FAZIO: -- I suspect that they would be very useful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: These are Prosecutor's notes? MR. DI FAZIO: These are investigators' notes headed "Informal Statement," and as I understand and read them, they are notes taken by investigators, reduced to writing, and provided to the Defence. Now, I'm certain they --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: They're dated ... MR. DI FAZIO: July 19, 1998.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Under -- MR. DI FAZIO: Present was a gentleman named John Mikulic [phoen] and Yves Roy, investigator from the OTP.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Do you have any -- as far as the Prosecution is concerned, you are saying that they were handed to the Defence. MR. DI FAZIO: As I stand here I haven't done a check on this particular document, but I understand that from the investigations made last night that this is one of the sets of material disclosed to the Defence. It's important, of course, that we ascertain that it's all been disclosed and that the Defence are aware of it, because it's important to them to know. And secondly, it might affect the way that Mr. Lazarevic conducts his cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: I can well understand that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah. Because we've been through this problem before -- MR. DI FAZIO: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: -- of handing in a bunch of documents without identifying each one of them and also without having anybody sign for their receipt. MR. DI FAZIO: Well, I can go and check this specific document, but the issue arose yesterday, as you know, when Mr. Pantelic asked, "Do we have all the documents," and the search was conducted, and as far as I am aware, this is a document that was handed to the Defence, these particular notes taken in 1998. If you want me to say to you I have investigated and looked at our records and have got evidence that they were disclosed, then I would need time to do that, but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because the way the Defence's position is that they were never given any document it's up to the Prosecution to show that on this date they were delivered by so-and-so and received by so-and-so, because that's the way the parties are supposed to handle documents. MR. DI FAZIO: With respect, I entirely agree. With respect, I entirely agree. It's a question of my being able to do it at this particular moment as I stand here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So Mr. Lazarevic's position is that you have never received the notes by the investigators dated 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. This is exactly the position of Mr. Zaric's defence. I have just spoke with Mr. Pisarevic. He never received it. Also, I spoke to all the Defence counsels, and I have seen the sign that was given to us by --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: The defendants, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- all the defendants, and they have never seen anything like that. And this brings me into a pretty difficult situation -- MR. DI FAZIO: It does. It does.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- to continue with this cross-examination, because I really don't feel good about asserting something to the witness that is not correct and something that I don't know about. So maybe it would be helpful just for this moment for my learned colleague to show us these exact papers, just to examine them briefly in these few minutes just to see what it's about, and then there are very few more questions that I have to ask this witness. Maybe there is -- it is not of that importance for this moment, but generally the problem remains. MR. DI FAZIO: I entirely agree with what Mr. Lazarevic says. It's important for him to have the material because obviously it's the way he constructs his cross-examination is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yeah, and also the credibility of the witness. MR. DI FAZIO: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Because if an incident which appears to be important is only mentioned very late, then the implication is that it's an afterthought. MR. DI FAZIO: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: So it's not fair to the witness either. MR. DI FAZIO: It's not fair to the witness, and it's not fair to the Defence, and it's not fair to us. So it's a matter that needs to be sorted out.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. I hope Mr. Lazarevic can look through and perhaps -- unless he needs more time.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I please confer for one minute with other counsel, because now I believe that now we do have some problems --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, yes. You go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- which enables me to continue with this cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, the Prosecutors or the investigators' notes do not have any evidentiary value as far as the trial is concerned, so that counsel can go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I am fully aware of that, but there are some information that -- well, for example, if I ask the witness this was the first time that you said this and in this situation, it was obvious that it wasn't the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, on the other hand, I can confirm now, on seeing this document, that this is the first time that I and all other Defence counsel sees this document. [redacted]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [redacted] So would this be considered as his informal statement or notes taken by the investigators or Prosecutor's side, I still cannot figure all that. And on the other hand -- please excuse me. I really believe that I need to show this document to my client, because this is something that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You have to get instructions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- to get instructions because otherwise I really don't feel it would be appropriate for me to continue with cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes, because it may raise some important issues regarding the defence of your client.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Whether or not the Prosecution verifies as to what date -- verifies that the notes were taken at the time they say they were taken, you can understand the problem Mr. Lazarevic has raised. MR. DI FAZIO: Oh, I do. I do. I do understand. And I raised it because I could see the way the cross-examination was going and it puzzled me, and because of that I raised the issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe -- MR. DI FAZIO: It's important he has those notes and he gets instructions on those notes, and it's important from our point of view, of course, to check whether or not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Yes. MR. DI FAZIO: -- we've disclosed it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, how much time do you think you need?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe some 30 minutes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I apologise, Your Honour. Maybe some 20 to 30 minutes, nothing more than that. That's my estimation of finishing this cross-examination. Also, maybe some new questions. Maybe I'll have to go back to some issues after I check this, but I can assure the Court that it wouldn't take much more than 20 to 30 minutes, although I cannot be 100 per cent sure.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: No. That's the time you need to consult with your client, is it, or that's the time --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: That is -- that was actually the time that I had to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: To cross-examine --

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- for cross-examination. But I believe that by tomorrow I will be able to examine all these with my client and then tomorrow --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: You may finish.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: -- then I can go with this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: All right. So in that case, we'll just have to adjourn and continue tomorrow. Yes, Mr. Weiner.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: Your Honour, could we go into private session for a matter --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. WEINER
utterances.text: -- unrelated to this?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: Oh, I see. Okay. So the cross-examination is adjourned until tomorrow at 1415.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: And maybe the witness could leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: We'll go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MUMBA
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Thursday, the 17th day of January, 2002, at 2.15 p.m. 25
